teaser: Some things stick. Some slide. How far can a pull reach?
title: Fridge Magnets
question: What sticks, what slides off, and how far can the pull reach?
idea: A magnet pulls on some metals. The pull is stronger close by and weaker farther away.

curiosity.intro: A little tug at the fridge opens a kitchen full of questions.
curiosity.carryForward: Try one surface, change one thing, and notice what happens.

questions.question: What holds a magnet to the fridge?
questions.notice: Look at the magnet holding the paper drawing.
questions.say: The magnet and the steel in this fridge door pull toward each other. The pull helps the magnet stay put. It can act through a thin piece of paper; the paper does not have to be magnetic.
questions.try: Point to the magnet, the paper, and the steel door. Tell which two pull toward each other.

questions.question: Will it stick to every surface?
questions.notice: The magnet rests at the bottom of the wood board.
questions.say: Magnets stick to some metals, including iron and many kinds of steel. They do not stick to wood, plastic, paper, or cloth. Aluminum foil and copper do not stick to an ordinary fridge magnet either.
questions.try: With Big nearby, predict and try a few fridge magnets on a fridge door or steel cookie sheet and a tray of paper, a plastic lid, wood, aluminum foil, and a steel paperclip. Notice what sticks and what slides. Keep magnets away from screens, cards with stripes, and mouths.

questions.question: How far can the pull reach?
questions.notice: Look for the tiny gap beside the paperclip.
questions.say: A magnetic pull can act across a gap. The closer the magnet is, the stronger the pull. Farther away, it gets weaker. Different magnets and objects can give different results.
questions.try: With Big beside you, slowly move a magnet toward a steel paperclip on a tray. Use a ruler or finger-widths to compare the gap where it first moves. Lift the paperclip a little with the magnet, then gently draw them apart over the tray until it lets go.

questions.question: Can two magnets push apart?
questions.notice: Look at the two ends facing each other.
questions.say: Two magnets can pull together or push apart. Turning one magnet can change which ends face each other, changing the pull to a push.
questions.try: With Big, turn one of two large magnets around and notice whether they pull together or push apart.

reading.title: Follow the pull
reading.coverText: A fridge door, a small gap, and a pull to explore.
reading.foldableCoverLine: Some things stick. Some things slide.
reading.foldableNote: Keep a question from the kitchen.
reading.parentNote: Age 8 / Grade 3 reading. Welcome spoken answers and dictation. Use the story to explain magnet, stick, pull, metal, fridge, and slide.

beats.title: A small kitchen mystery
beats.passage: Little Wonderer noticed a round magnet on the fridge. It stayed in place without a hand holding it. A magnet is an object that can pull certain metals toward it. Little brought the magnifier closer. “What makes it stick?” Big Wonderer stood beside Little, ready to look for clues.
beats.prompt: What clue suggests a pull can act before things touch?

foldable.heading: A kitchen mystery
foldable.body: Little found a magnet on the fridge. It stayed without a hand holding it. What could be pulling it toward the door?

beats.title: A pull that holds
beats.passage: Big lifted the magnet, then brought it close to the door. Little felt a tug before it touched. The magnet and the steel in this fridge door pulled toward each other. That pull helped it stick, or stay in place. A paper drawing stayed between them, even though the paper itself was not magnetic.
beats.prompt: Why can a magnet hold paper to a steel door without pulling on the paper itself?

foldable.heading: A pull that holds
foldable.body: The magnet and steel door pulled toward each other. Their pull held a paper drawing, though the paper itself was not magnetic.

beats.title: Try another surface
beats.passage: Would the same magnet stick everywhere? Big held up a wood board over a tray. The magnet began to slide, moving down the smooth surface. It did not stick to the plastic lid, paper, or cloth either. Shiny aluminum foil did not hold it. “Metal is not one kind of stuff,” Little noticed.
beats.prompt: How did the foil test change the idea that all metal sticks?

foldable.heading: Some things slide
foldable.body: The magnet slid down the wood. Plastic and foil did not hold it either. Little found that only some metals stick.

beats.title: A pull across a gap
beats.passage: Big set a steel paperclip on the tray, then moved the magnet nearer. Little watched the paperclip tip toward it across a small gap. Closer made the pull stronger. Farther away made it weaker. They moved slowly and checked the gap with a ruler. The distance that worked depended on this magnet and this paperclip.
beats.prompt: How could you check whether moving closer changes the pull?

foldable.heading: Across a small gap
foldable.body: A steel paperclip tipped toward the magnet. Closer made the pull stronger. Farther away made it weaker. Little checked the gap.

beats.title: Turn and try again
beats.passage: Big brought out a second magnet. One way round, the magnets pulled together with a little snap. Big turned one around. Now their facing ends pushed apart. Little tried to bring them closer and felt the push. The same two magnets could pull or push, depending on how their ends faced.
beats.prompt: What changed when Big turned one magnet around?

foldable.heading: Turn and try again
foldable.body: Two magnets pulled together. Big turned one around, and their ends pushed apart. Little could feel that turning changed the pull.

beats.title: A question to keep
beats.passage: Little drew the fridge, the wood board, and the paperclip in a notebook. “Some things stick. Some slide. And a pull can cross a gap!” Big nodded. Little left room for one more question: “What sticks, what slides off, and how far can the pull reach?”
beats.prompt: Which test would you repeat to learn how far the pull reaches?

foldable.heading: Keep a question
foldable.body: Little drew the tests in a notebook. What sticks, what slides off, and how far can the pull reach? There was more to try.

writing.title: Give your magnet test its words
writing.intro: Say one clear command, then draw or write it.
writing.draw: Draw a magnet near the fridge or a steel paperclip. Show the gap.

frames.hint: tell where to hold the magnet

writing.parentNote: Welcome speech, dictation, invented spelling, or writing. One command is enough. Example: “Hold the magnet near the fridge, then slowly pull it away and notice when it lets go.”

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: The magnet and steel door pull toward each other through the thin paper. Paper alone does not attract the magnet.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: Wood and aluminum foil did not hold the magnet. The evidence shows it sticks to some materials and some metals, not all of them.

answers.label: Reading · 3
answers.text: The paperclip tipped toward the magnet when it came closer. Moving farther away made the pull too weak to keep it lifted.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept a clear command spoken, dictated, drawn, or written. Example: “Hold the magnet near the fridge, then slowly pull it away and notice when it lets go.”

parentGuidance: Age 8, Grade 3 reading, Grade 2 math. A grown-up stays nearby, chooses large intact fridge magnets, and leads the tray activity. Keep magnets away from screens, cards with stripes, and mouths. Use a steel fridge door or cookie sheet; some stainless-steel doors do not hold magnets. Iron and many steels attract strongly; ordinary fridge magnets do not stick to aluminum or copper. Paper, wood, plastic, and cloth are nonmagnetic test surfaces, though a thin layer can let a magnet hold against steel behind it. The magnet and steel attract each other; friction helps keep the magnet from sliding down the door. The diorama shows a qualitative comparison, not a measured range or force: its slider has near/far positions, and the contact test shows whether this magnet stays on the selected surface. Real reach depends on the magnet, object, gap, and friction. Two magnets can attract or repel depending on which poles face; flat fridge magnets may have several alternating poles, so use a pair of large bar magnets for the optional turning test.

questions.prompt: Why does this magnet stay on the steel fridge door?
choices: The magnet and steel pull toward each other
questions.answer: The magnet and steel door pull toward each other, helping the magnet stay in place.

questions.prompt: Which object is most likely to stick to a fridge magnet?
questions.answer: A steel paperclip is attracted to a fridge magnet. Magnets stick to some metals, not all metals.

questions.prompt: What usually happens as the magnet moves farther from the paperclip?
questions.answer: The pull gets weaker as the magnet moves farther from the paperclip.

questions.prompt: What can happen when you turn one of two magnets around?
choices: A pull can change to a push
questions.answer: Turning one magnet can change a pull to a push because different ends face each other.
